questions.prompt: Linearization of \(\dot x = f(x, u)\) about an equilibrium \((x_e, u_e)\) replaces \(f\) by
questions.explanation: The first-order Taylor expansion is \(\delta\dot x = A\,\delta x + B\,\delta u\), with \(A\) and \(B\) the partial derivatives at the equilibrium. \(f(x_e, u_e)\) is zero by the definition of equilibrium, so it does not describe the motion. The linear model is local, not exact on the whole state space. The second derivative is the next term, the one the linear model drops.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>jacobian entries</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">df/dx   df/du</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A row of two partial derivatives.
options: its Jacobian in \(x\) and in \(u\), and is accurate for small deviations
the value \(f(x_e, u_e)\), which is the whole story for large deviations too
a linear model that is exact for every initial state
the second derivative only, ignoring the slope

questions.prompt: The scalar system is \(\dot x = -x^3 + u\). It rests at \(x = 2\), which needs \(u = 8\). The linearized \(A = \partial f/\partial x\) there is
questions.explanation: \(\partial f/\partial x = -3x^2\). At \(x = 2\) that is \(-12\), so \(A = -12\). The value \(-3x = -6\) drops one factor of \(x\). The equilibrium input 8 is \(u_e\), not the Jacobian.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>jacobian entries</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">df/dx   df/du</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A row of two partial derivatives.

questions.prompt: For the same \(\dot x = -x^3 + u\), the input Jacobian \(B = \partial f/\partial u\) is
questions.explanation: The input enters as \(+u\), so \(B = 1\) at every state. Using \(A = -12\) as if it were \(B\) mixes the two partial derivatives. Using \(u_e = 8\) reports the equilibrium input instead of the slope in \(u\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>jacobian entries</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">df/dx   df/du</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A row of two partial derivatives.

questions.prompt: A tank obeys \(\dot h = -2\sqrt{h} + q\). It rests at \(h = 9\). The linearized coefficient of \(\delta h\) is
questions.explanation: The derivative of \(-2 h^{1/2}\) is \(-h^{-1/2} = -1/3\) at \(h = 9\), so \(A = -0.333333\). The outflow \(-2\sqrt{9} = -6\) is the equilibrium flow, not the slope. Half of that slope, \(-1/6\), comes from differentiating \(\sqrt{h}\) and forgetting the constant 2, or from differentiating and then dividing an extra time.

questions.prompt: The equilibrium of a smooth nonlinear system is locally asymptotically stable when
questions.explanation: Local asymptotic stability follows when the linearization is asymptotically stable and no eigenvalue sits on the imaginary axis. One stable eigenvalue is not enough if another has a positive real part. The zero matrix is a critical case, not a stable one. A single equilibrium can still be unstable.

every eigenvalue of the Jacobian has a negative real part

questions.prompt: A pendulum linearizes, near the bottom, to \(\ddot\theta + (g/L)\theta = 0\) with \(g/L = 10\). The natural frequency of that small motion is
questions.explanation: The standard form is \(\ddot\theta + \omega_n^2\theta = 0\), so \(\omega_n = \sqrt{g/L} = \sqrt{10} = 3.16228\). The ratio \(g/L = 10\) is \(\omega_n^2\), not \(\omega_n\). Half of 10 is not the square root.

questions.prompt: The Jacobian test is inconclusive when
questions.explanation: An eigenvalue with zero real part is the critical case: the linear terms do not decide stability, and the nonlinear terms can go either way. A full set of open-left-half-plane eigenvalues is conclusive and says locally stable. A zero input is just a choice of coordinates. Dimension 2 is ordinary and not a special case.

questions.prompt: Near the origin, \(\dot x_1 = x_2\) and \(\dot x_2 = -2 x_1 + 0.5 x_2^2 + u\). The determinant of the Jacobian \(A\) is
questions.explanation: The quadratic term \(0.5 x_2^2\) has zero derivative at the origin, so \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Its determinant is \(2\), stored as 2. The trace is 0, which is not the determinant. The entry \(-2\) is one corner of \(A\), not \(\det A\).

questions.prompt: Return to \(\dot x = -x^3 + u\), now at the equilibrium \(x = 1.5\). The state Jacobian \(A\) is
questions.explanation: \(A = -3x^2 = -3\cdot 2.25 = -6.75\). The value at \(x = 2\), which is \(-12\), belongs to a different equilibrium. The equilibrium input \(u = x^3 = 3.375\) is not \(A\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>jacobian entries</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">df/dx   df/du</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A row of two partial derivatives.

questions.prompt: The system \(\dot x = x(1-x) + u\) rests at \(x = 3\). The linearized \(A\) is
questions.explanation: \(f = x - x^2 + u\), so \(A = 1 - 2x = 1 - 6 = -5\). The factor \(1 - x = -2\) forgets the product rule and is not the derivative of \(x - x^2\). The equilibrium input, which is 6, is \(u_e\), not \(A\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>local linear poles</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="123" y1="41" x2="133" y2="51" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="51" x2="133" y2="41" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="129" x2="133" y2="139" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="139" x2="133" y2="129" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A complex pair of pole marks in the left half-plane.

questions.explanation: Each equilibrium has its own Jacobian, so a scheduled controller carries several local models and interpolates among them. One model is ordinary linear control. Exact cancellation of the nonlinearity is feedback linearization, a different construction. The equilibria are exactly where each local model is built.

questions.prompt: The scalar system \(\dot x = x - x^3\) has an equilibrium at \(x = 1\). The Jacobian there is
questions.explanation: \(A = 1 - 3x^2\). At \(x = 1\), \(A = -2\). At the origin the same formula gives \(+1\), which is the unstable equilibrium, not this one. The value \(-3x = -3\) drops a factor of \(x\).
